title: Blind guides (Luke 6:39–49)
hook: a good person out of the good treasure of the heart brings good
carry: out of the heart the mouth speaks

segments.voice: Yesterday, the grain market and the heaped measure. Your line was running over. What did you give the heaped version of, and did anything spill back? Day five hundred twenty-five.

"Can the blind lead the blind? shall they not both fall into the ditch?" Jesus says it almost like a riddle, the kind of saying you'd hear at a village well. It's the last stretch of the sermon on the plain, and the tone changes. After the big things, love your enemies, give with a heaped measure, he turns to something closer to home: the people who try to guide others. Parents. Teachers. Bosses. Friends who give advice. Anyone who's ever said here's what you should do. Which is everyone. And he offers a handful of quick pictures, one after another, like snapshots from a working village: a ditch, a speck of dust, a fig tree, a storehouse, a house in a flood.
screen: `A DITCH, A SPECK, A TREE, A HOUSE.`

segments.voice: First, the speck: "And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but perceivest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" A mote is a speck of dust. A beam is a wooden roof beam. The picture is meant to be funny: a man with a plank sticking out of his face, squinting at his friend's eyelash. Fix your own sight first, then you can help. Second, the tree. Good trees bear good fruit. "For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes." You don't judge a tree by its label; you judge it by what grows on it. Third, the heart, and today's center: "A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil: for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh." Treasure here is thesauros, a storehouse, the place where you keep things. Whatever you've been storing up comes out when you open your mouth, especially when you're tired or surprised. Words are the fruit; the heart is the tree. And finally the house. Someone who hears and does is like a man who "digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock." The flood comes, and the house stands. Someone who hears and doesn't do built on bare earth, and the flood takes it. So the blind guide isn't someone without sight in their eyes. It's someone who hasn't looked inward, whose storehouse is empty, who talks without doing.
screen: `A TREE IS KNOWN BY ITS FRUIT.`
then, large: `OF THE ABUNDANCE OF THE HEART HIS MOUTH SPEAKETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak from the good in you. Settle, and breathe. Picture your heart as a storehouse, shelves and barrels. What have you been storing this week? Worry, resentment, gratitude, a kind thing someone said, a grudge, a song. Look honestly. Then think of the words that came out of you lately, especially the quick ones. Do you recognize where they came from? Now find something good on those shelves: a memory of kindness, a person you admire, something that made you laugh. Hold it for a few breaths. That's the treasure you want your words to come from today. If you pray, you can ask for a good storehouse. If you don't, simply rest with the good thing you found. The bell holds the time.
Blind guides. Jesus' warning about guiding others without looking inward first, and his picture of words coming out of the storehouse of the heart.

Your line: out of the heart the mouth speaks. Before you give advice today, check for a beam in your own eye. And look back at the week: a breaking net, a hole in a roof, new wine, a night of prayer, the plain, a heaped measure, a storehouse. Day five hundred twenty-five, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Christians often quote the mote and the beam as a check before judging others, and the house built on the rock is a familiar Sunday school song and sermon picture.

myth: the mote and the beam is meant to be a little funny
a man with a plank in his eye squinting at a speck in his friend's.
Luke's wise builder simply built on a rock
Luke says he digged deep and laid the foundation on a rock.
thesauros means a storehouse, where you keep things.

fork.setup: you notice a speck in your friend's eye and want to help. what does Jesus say to do first?
options: take the beam out of your own eye.
fork.reveal: first cast out the beam from your own eye; then you'll see clearly to help with your friend's speck.

original.note: Greek: a treasure, or the storehouse where treasure is kept. English gets thesaurus from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: good people say nice things.
what it means: words come out of what we've stored up in the heart, so the work starts inside, before the mouth.
what a scholar hears: thesauros is the storehouse itself, the same word that gives English "thesaurus," a storehouse of words.
recall: Latin for magnify, the song's first word
